name: Web Fundamentals
description: How a page loads, the browser rendering pipeline, storage, the same-origin policy, CORS and Core Web Vitals.

modules.name: Loading & Rendering
modules.description: What happens between typing a URL and seeing pixels.

cards.prompt: Walk through what happens when you type a URL and press Enter.
cards.answer: DNS resolution → TCP (or QUIC) connection → TLS handshake → HTTP request → response → HTML parsed into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite. Subresources are fetched as the parser discovers them, and JavaScript may block parsing.
cards.explanation: This question is really about depth: any single step (DNS caching, TLS session resumption, HTTP/2 multiplexing, the preload scanner, critical rendering path) can be expanded. Knowing the shape tells you where a slow page is actually losing time.

resources.title: MDN — Populating the page: how browsers work

cards.answer: Plain scripts block parsing; `defer` downloads in parallel and runs after parsing in document order; `async` downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it lands, in any order.

left.title: defer
points: The right default for app code

cards.explanation: A blocking script in `<head>` stalls the parser, delaying first paint. `type="module"` is deferred by default. Anything that must run before paint (theme flash prevention) is the rare legitimate blocking script — keep it inline and tiny.

cards.prompt: What are the Core Web Vitals and their 'good' thresholds?
cards.answer: LCP (largest contentful paint) ≤ 2.5 s, INP (interaction to next paint) ≤ 200 ms, CLS (cumulative layout shift) ≤ 0.1.
cards.explanation: LCP is usually a slow hero image or a render-blocking resource; INP is long JavaScript tasks blocking the main thread; CLS is images and ads without reserved space. Fixes in order: set width/height on media, break up long tasks, preload the LCP resource.

cards.answer: SSR sends HTML the browser can paint immediately; CSR sends a shell plus JavaScript that builds the page in the browser.

left.title: SSR / SSG
points: Fast first paint and reliable SEO
Hydration cost to make it interactive

right.title: CSR
points: Blank until JS parses and runs
Weaker on slow devices and networks

cards.explanation: Modern frameworks blend them: static generation for stable pages, streaming SSR for dynamic ones, client components only where interaction lives. The deciding question is whether the first paint must be meaningful without JavaScript.

modules.name: Storage, Origins & Security
modules.description: Cookies, storage APIs, same-origin policy, CORS and CSP.

cards.prompt: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage vs IndexedDB
cards.answer: Cookies are sent with every matching request; the storage APIs are client-only. localStorage persists, sessionStorage dies with the tab, IndexedDB stores large structured data asynchronously.

left.title: Cookies
points: The thing consent banners are about

right.title: Web storage / IndexedDB
points: Never sent to the server automatically
Readable by any script on the origin — not for secrets

cards.explanation: Session tokens belong in HttpOnly cookies so XSS cannot read them. Anything in localStorage is exposed to every script you load — which is also why a privacy notice should mention local storage, not only cookies.

cards.prompt: What is an origin, and what does the same-origin policy prevent?
cards.answer: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port). The same-origin policy stops a document from reading data from another origin — its DOM, its responses, its storage — while still allowing embedding and navigation.
cards.explanation: It is the foundation of browser security: without it, any page could read your webmail in another tab. Note it blocks *reading*, not *sending* — which is exactly the gap CSRF exploits and SameSite cookies close.

cards.prompt: Your fetch fails with a CORS error. What is actually happening, and where do you fix it?
cards.answer: The browser made the request but refused to expose the response because the server did not send an appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The fix belongs on the server, never in the browser.
cards.explanation: A preflight `OPTIONS` is sent first for non-simple requests (custom headers, methods beyond GET/POST/HEAD, JSON content type). Credentialed requests require an explicit origin — not `*` — plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. CORS relaxes the same-origin policy; it is not a security control on your data.

cards.prompt: What does a Content Security Policy do, and what makes one actually effective?
cards.answer: It tells the browser which sources may load and execute — scripts, styles, frames, connections. An effective policy is nonce- or hash-based with `strict-dynamic`, avoids `unsafe-inline` and `unsafe-eval`, and sets `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'self'`.
cards.explanation: CSP is defence in depth: it turns many XSS bugs into blocked script loads. Host allowlists are weak — a single CDN with an open JSONP endpoint defeats them — which is why Google's guidance moved to nonces. Roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.

cards.prompt: A session cookie should be `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=___` to block script access, plaintext transport and most cross-site sends.
cards.explanation: `SameSite=Lax` is the modern default: sent on top-level navigations but not on cross-site subrequests, which kills most CSRF. Use `Strict` for high-value actions, and `None; Secure` only when a cookie genuinely must cross sites — as in embedded third-party contexts.
